clue.text: Nine preset switches? That's far from straightforward

indicators.note: to switch things round is to change their places, so these letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about rearranging nine settings, complaining that it is anything but simple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switches' looks like a noun (the nine preset switches on a panel) but is a verb telling you to rearrange NINE PRESET.
explanation.definitionFit: Something serpentine winds like a snake, so it is twisting and hardly direct.

clue.text: School arranged something for kids' amusement

parts.note: to school someone is to train them
set, as in set out or put in order

explanation.surface: A school organised some entertainment for the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' reads as a noun but is the verb, to coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A model railway layout is a classic toy that children play with.

clue.text: Start given to European entertainer

parts.note: dawn is the start of the day, or the beginning of anything
French people are Europeans

explanation.surface: A European performer gets a break at the beginning of a career.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn French is a British comedian and actress, known for The Vicar of Dibley and her double act with Jennifer Saunders.
explanation.definitionFit: She is a well-known British comic performer, so she is an example of an entertainer.

clue.text: Touched cloth

definitions.meaning: past tense of the verb meaning to sense by contact with the hand
a matted woollen fabric, as used for hats and pool tables

explanation.surface: Someone handled a piece of fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the past tense of feel, to touch; the other is the pressed woollen material.

clue.text: Struggle with expectation

parts.note: to vie is to compete or strive

explanation.surface: Someone battles against what others hope of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The sense of expectation is the one in phrases like 'with a view to' or 'in view of', meaning an intention or prospect.
explanation.definitionFit: A view can be an outlook or prospect, what one anticipates or intends happening.

clue.text: Type of locks in frame of doors protecting study

indicators.note: the outer letters surround and so guard the piece placed between them
the frame of a word is its outer edge, so only the first and last letters of doors are kept

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to study it

explanation.surface: A sort of door lock fitted inside the doorframe of a study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks' pretends to be the hardware on a door; it is hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreadlocks, shortened, are a style of matted, rope-like hair, so they are a kind of tresses.

clue.text: Long lead taken from back of Macintosh

indicators.note: the lead letter is the first one, and it is removed from the spelt-out name

parts.note: the last letter of Macintosh is H, here written out in full as the letter's name

explanation.surface: A long cable has been removed from behind a Mac computer.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter H, at the back of Macintosh, must be spelt out as AITCH before its first letter goes; the clue gives no sign of that spelling-out, so this is a tough step.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn or be impatient for it, as in being eager to go.

clue.text: Junior Scout putting away a very alcoholic drink

indicators.note: something put away is removed from sight, so these letters come out of the word

parts.note: Beavers are the youngest section of the Scout Association in the UK
A, plus V as the usual abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A young scout is downing a very strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Beavers are the UK scouting section for children aged about six to eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale and lager are brewed from malt and hops and contain alcohol, so a pint is one such drink.

clue.text: French film featuring old artist — tons better!

indicators.note: a film featuring something includes it, so these letters go inside the title

parts.note: Amélie is a 2001 French romantic comedy
RA, Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A French movie starring an elderly painter is a vast improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: ORAT goes in between the I and the final E of AMELIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ameliorate is to improve something or make it better, a verb sense of the word.

clue.text: Choose to get involved, having zero alternative

indicators.note: having means holding or containing, so the phrase's letters hold the zero inside them

parts.note: to opt in is to choose to take part
the figure 0 resembles the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone decides to join in because there is no other choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' puts O inside OPTIN, between the I and the N. 'zero alternative' looks like a phrase meaning no choice, but 'alternative' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An option is one choice among several, which is exactly what an alternative is.

clue.text: Prince wearing two hats, strangely, for riverside walks

indicators.note: the scrambled letters are worn round the inner piece like clothing, enclosing it
these words appear in an odd, unusual order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A royal wearing two hats at once is odd attire for strolls by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' scrambles TWO HATS to TOWATHS, and 'wearing' puts P inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Towpaths run along canals and rivers, once used by horses hauling boats, and are now used for walking.

clue.text: Tattoos damaged skin

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tattoos have harmed someone's skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tattoos' looks like a plural noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To tattoo someone is to mark their body with dye, so it means to put pigment into the skin.

clue.text: Correspondent recollected heartless perversions

indicators.note: read as re-collected, gathered together again in a new order
the heart of a word is its central letter, which is dropped here

explanation.surface: A letter writer recalled cruel acts of depravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes R, the middle letter of PERVERSIONS, leaving PERVESIONS; 'recollected' rearranges it. 'Correspondent' is the adjective, not the letter writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Correspondent can mean answering or matching in reply, which is what reacting readily implies; both words come from roots meaning to answer.

clue.text: Glasses chip at the bottom in short amounts of time

indicators.note: the chosen letter goes inside the abbreviated time units

parts.note: secs is short for seconds

indicators.note: in a down entry, the bottom of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Spectacles get chipped on the lower rim within moments.
explanation.walkthrough: Specs is informal for spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses worn on the face to correct eyesight are spectacles, informally shortened.

clue.text: Study of deep space?

parts.note: sounds like astronomy, but the deep is a poetic name for the sea, and its space is the vast expanse of water

explanation.surface: A question about the science of the far reaches of the universe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deep space' reads as outer space; 'the deep' is the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the science of the seas, their waters, life and floors, so it studies the deep.

clue.text: Criminally bad football team introduces international talent

indicators.note: the club's name comes first and leads in what follows it

parts.note: Aston Villa, an English Premier League club, often shortened to Villa
nous is practical intelligence or know-how

explanation.surface: A football club, dreadful at the game, brings in a gifted foreign player.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club, usually just called Villa.
explanation.definitionFit: A villainous act is wicked, the work of a crook, so the word means criminally bad.

clue.text: Duke is protected by fort

indicators.note: the fort's letters surround and guard the inner word

explanation.surface: A nobleman is kept safe inside a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' looks like a nobleman, but 'dukes' is slang for fists, as in 'put up your dukes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes is old slang for the hands clenched for boxing, so a duke is a clenched hand.

clue.text: Relative from Spain visiting somewhere in France

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so this letter enters the town

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: A family member from Spain is staying in a French town.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a family member.

clue.text: Young hoodlums finally leaving shopping centre

indicators.note: one letter departs from the word

parts.note: the small, meaning small children, the young

indicators.note: the last letter of hoodlums is used

explanation.surface: Teenage thugs eventually walk out of the shopping precinct.
explanation.definitionFit: A mall is a covered complex of shops, the American term for a shopping precinct.

clue.text: Suspect type of card set up with credit

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: a SIM card goes in a mobile phone
to credit something is to believe it, to trust it

explanation.surface: Someone is wary of a kind of card arranged with a credit facility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' is a verb here, to doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspect someone is to doubt them, to feel a lack of confidence in them.

clue.text: Authority figure wanting a pipe and new trousers

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is missing from the word

parts.note: a leader is someone in charge
a hose is a flexible pipe

explanation.surface: A boss wants a pipe to smoke and a new pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Lederhosen are leather shorts traditionally worn in Bavaria and Austria.
explanation.definitionFit: These are leather breeches from Alpine tradition, so they are a kind of legwear.

clue.text: Incredibly wayward serve gets over

indicators.note: something wayward goes astray, so these letters stray into another order

parts.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A wildly off-target tennis serve goes long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredibly' looks like an anagram signal; it is the definition, and 'wayward' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever so is an informal intensifier meaning very, extremely, as in 'ever so kind'.

clue.text: Criticise guys going round taking ecstasy

indicators.note: taking here means taking away, so a letter is removed
turning round makes the word read backwards

parts.note: guys are men, males
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Condemn the men who are passing round ecstasy pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' turns MALES into SELAM; 'taking' then removes its E. 'Taking ecstasy' wants to mean adding E, but it takes it away.
explanation.definitionFit: To slam something is to criticise it harshly, as a reviewer might pan a play.

clue.text: Beers consumed by damn stupid bloke from Richmond?

indicators.note: the beers are swallowed up inside the other letters
a stupid arrangement is a senseless one, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: ales are beers

explanation.surface: A man from Richmond downs pints with a foolish curse.
explanation.walkthrough: Richmond here is the market town in North Yorkshire, in the Yorkshire Dales, not the London suburb; the question mark marks the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A man from the Yorkshire Dales is so called, and Richmond is one of their towns.

clue.text: Co-worker is friendly, though not at first

indicators.note: the opening letter is missing from the word

parts.note: pally means friendly, like a pal

explanation.surface: A colleague turns out to be friendly, after a cool start.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally works together with you toward a shared aim, so is a collaborator.

clue.text: Bacon, for one, made extremely vacuous art

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, so only those of made are kept
a vacuous word is empty, its middle letters gone, so art keeps only its ends

explanation.surface: Francis Bacon produced art that was utterly empty.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the painter Francis Bacon, but the definition is breakfast bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon is cured pork, an example of flesh eaten as food.

clue.text: Awkward person regularly in tears on date

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other letter

explanation.surface: A socially clumsy person keeps crying on a date.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerd is a socially inept, often studious person, so a gauche individual.

clue.text: Big cat biting a rabbit's head and part of the throat

indicators.note: the cat's letters close round the others like jaws

parts.note: a lynx is a wild cat

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A wild cat sinks its teeth into a rabbit's head and throat.
explanation.definitionFit: The voice box sits in the throat, so it is one part of it.

clue.text: Coke possibly seen as college guard prepared to arrest girl

indicators.note: an arrest holds someone, so these letters take in the girl
prepared means made ready, worked into shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A security officer at a college is ready to detain a young woman found with cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coke' looks like the soft drink, but cocaine is meant; 'possibly' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocaine falls into the most serious UK category of controlled substances, so it is one example.

clue.text: Corporations rejected rude material

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a corporation is a jocular term for a pot belly, so corporations are tums

explanation.surface: Big companies turned down obscene content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporations' looks like companies, but is old slang for big bellies.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is indecent writing or pictures, obscene content.
